title: Permissions in a scheduling product
excerpt: Show each person what they can do with a booking, and why a control is unavailable. Hidden actions feel like bugs, even when the server is right to refuse them.
alt: Crates of used books at an outdoor stall, titles facing out, each one labeled so you can tell what you are allowed to take.
caption: What you can reach should be readable from the aisle. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Who needs a role in a scheduling product?
faqs.answer: Start with the guest, the host, and anyone who acts for the host. Add a teammate, an assistant, or an owner when a real person is blocked every week. Each role needs one sentence about what they came to do. Permissions that serve none of those sentences are clutter.

faqs.question: Should unavailable actions be hidden?
faqs.answer: Hide an action the person would never look for, such as a guest editing the host's hours. If they will look for it, leave it visible or disabled and say why. A cancel rule, a private note, or a teammate's calendar needs a sentence at the point of the tap.

faqs.question: What should a public booking link reveal?
faqs.answer: It should reveal the open times you chose to publish, and the person or team the link promised. It should not reveal other guests' names, reasons, or private notes. Assistants can act for a host without becoming that host, and the invite should still name the host.

markdown:
Clear scheduling product permissions ux shows each person what they can do, and a plain reason when something is unavailable. A hidden button feels like a bug. A disabled button with no reason feels like one too.

The W3C's WCAG overview organizes its guidelines as perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A control someone cannot perceive, or cannot understand the limit of, fails that bar even when the server is correctly refusing the action.

## Name the roles before you draw the locks

A scheduling product usually has more than two people, and they do not want the same powers. Write the roles in the language of the work, then attach actions to them.

A typical set:

- Guest: see open times, take or request one, change or cancel within the host's rules.
- Host: set hours, accept or decline requests, move a meeting, see the guest's answers.
- Teammate: cover a meeting, or see that a colleague is busy, without editing their hours.
- Owner: billing, the booking page address, who else has a seat.
- Assistant: schedule on someone else's behalf, without becoming that person.

If your product only has a guest and a host, say so, and do not invent an admin console "for later" that already confuses the first screens. Extra roles are cheap to name and expensive to leak. Add one when a real person is blocked every week, not because a permissions matrix looks complete.

Write one sentence per role: what they came to do. The guest came for a time. The host came to protect their week and still be findable. The assistant came to act for someone else without pretending to be them. Every permission should serve one of those sentences. A permission that serves none of them is a setting you will have to explain forever.

## Show the action, then the limit

If a guest can see a meeting but cannot cancel it, leave the meeting visible and say why the cancel action is missing. "Alex asks for 24 hours' notice to cancel. Write them if you need to move it." That is a rule. Removing the meeting from their list, or showing a button that fails with "forbidden," is a puzzle.

Disabled is allowed when the reason is next to it. Hidden is allowed when the action would be nonsense for this role, such as a guest editing the host's weekly hours. The test is whether a reasonable person would look for the control and think the product was broken when they cannot find it. Guests look for cancel. They do not look for "edit availability." Hide the second. Explain the first.

Do the same for the host looking at a teammate's calendar. "You can see that Jordan is busy. You cannot open the guest's notes." Busy is enough for scheduling around someone. The notes are a different trust. Say the boundary in the place they tapped, not in a help doc they will not open.

The W3C frames this as operable and understandable. The person should be able to perceive the control that is for them, operate it, and understand why a neighboring control is not. A tooltip that appears only on hover fails people using a keyboard or a phone. Put the reason in text that stays on the screen.

## Shared pages and private details

A public booking link is a permission decision you have already made. Anyone with the link can see the open times you chose to publish. Do not also publish the names of people who booked those times, the reasons they gave, or the gaps you marked as focus. Busy blocks can show as busy. The cause of the block stays with the host.

Team pages need an extra sentence. If the link promises "anyone on the support team," the visitor may land with a person they did not choose. Say that before they confirm. If the link promises a named person, do not silently substitute a colleague because of a round-robin rule the visitor never saw. Substitution can be a feature. It is a permission bug when it contradicts the link.

Internal notes on a booking are not part of the guest's record of the meeting. Keep them on the host's side of the screen, visually and in the data. A forwarded confirmation email should not contain "sounds difficult, keep it short." Review the email templates as if they were a permissions screen, because they are one. Whatever you render into the message, you have granted.

Assistants are the sharp case. They should be able to book, move, and cancel for the host, and the guest should see that the meeting is still with the host. The audit line can say the assistant made the change. The calendar invite should not come from the assistant's personal address unless that is what the host intended. Acting for someone is not the same as becoming them.

## Requests, holds, and who is allowed to say yes

Some products let a guest take a time directly. Some only let them request it. That is a permission, and it belongs in the button label, as the first screen of the product already had to promise. If a teammate may confirm requests for a colleague, show those requests in the teammate's queue and say whose calendar will receive the meeting.

Declining is a permission too. The host can decline. The guest should not be able to decline on the host's behalf. A mis-sent link that lets a guest hit Decline on someone else's request is a serious bug dressed up as a shortcut. Check the token in the email. A guest token and a host token should not be interchangeable because they look similar in the URL.

Holds are a quieter permission. The guest who started a form may hold a slot. Another guest should see it as taken, or as still free, according to a rule you state. They should not see who is holding it. The host may see the hold and may release it. A teammate probably should not release it unless they cover that calendar. Write this down next to the other roles so the empty-looking slot has an owner.

## When access changes

People leave teams. Assistants change. A founder stops sharing a calendar with a contractor. Permissions have to expire on purpose. Remove the seat, and say what happens to future meetings that person had booked for others. Past meetings can stay on the calendar as history. Their ability to edit next month should end when the seat ends.

Invite links should expire, and a used or expired link should explain itself. "This link has expired. Ask Alex for a new one." A blank 403, or a redirect to a signup page, makes the invited person think they did something wrong. You emailed them. The product should remember that.

If you let a host transfer a booking page to a new owner, confirm it in words, not only with a dropdown. Transferring ownership is closer to handing over a bank login than to changing a color. Name what moves: the public URL, the upcoming meetings, the connected calendar, the saved questions. Let them keep a copy of upcoming meetings even if the calendar connection has to be redone by the new owner.

## Leave a record a person can read

When someone changes a meeting, the product should say who did it, in the language of the roles, not as a user id. "Moved by Sam (assistant) on Tuesday." The host can see that. The guest can see the new time, and that it was updated, without a dump of internal seats. An audit line is a permission made visible after the fact. It is how you answer "who touched this" without giving everyone the right to touch it.

Keep that record on the booking, not only in a log the owner can export. The person staring at Thursday needs it there. A log no one opens will not settle the argument. A line under the time will.

If a role is view-only, say view-only in the header of the screen, not only by omitting buttons and hoping they notice. "You can see Jordan's week. You cannot change it." That sentence prevents a tour of the interface looking for a handle that is not there. It also prevents the bug report that would have followed.

## Build the checks where the action is

Check permission on the server when the action runs, and also shape the screen so people are not invited to try illegal actions all day. Both matter. A polished hidden button with a wide-open endpoint is not a permission model. An endpoint that returns "forbidden" under a button you still rendered, with no explanation, is not one either.

On a Hanabi project we write the role sentences before the screens, then design the unavailable states in Figma beside the available ones. The build, in Next.js, React, and TypeScript, should read the same rules the interface claims. Prisma and PostgreSQL are a sound place for the seat, the role, and the booking, so a permission is a query you can explain, not a pile of flags in the client.

The moment a person cannot find a meeting, a person, or a past booking, they will search. [Search inside a scheduling product](/blog/search-inside-a-scheduling-product) is the next decision, because search is what people open when the navigation, including the navigation of "what am I allowed to see," has already failed them.

If you want to see how a small product keeps private notes private and still lets a guest finish a task, look through [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful question on each project is what the screen allowed, and what it refused in plain language.
